Also there are cars and buildings, so the fight could be messier."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Today we read pp. 327–333, the fight itself. For *catapulted* (p. 327) and *deflected* (p. 327), look at the action around them. Something is thrown, something is turned aside. Now look at *disguised* (p. 328), *disbelief* (p. 330) and *disintegrate* (p. 331). Each starts with *dis-*, which can mean 'apart,' 'not,' or 'opposite.' Dis-believe is 'not believing'; dis-integrate is 'coming apart.'"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Using the *dis-* clue, what do you think *disintegrate* means on p. 331?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It means to come apart, like break into tiny pieces. The *dis-* means apart, and the sentence is about something falling to pieces."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Now the feeling and result words: *recede* (p. 330) means to move back or fade. *fled* (p. 331) means ran away. *hesitated* (p. 331) means paused out of doubt. *drained* (p. 332) means emptied of energy. *reclaimed* (p. 332) has the prefix *re-*, meaning 'again,' so it means got something back."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does the word *drained* help you picture Percy after the fight?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"*Drained* makes me think he has no energy left, like a cup that's been emptied. Today we sort details from the fight into three groups: Percy's injuries, Ares's attacks, and the mortals who step in. Then we ask what the details show about Percy as a hero."},{"type":"directions","text":"Reread pp. 327–333. Make a three-column chart labeled Percy's injuries, Ares's attacks, and Mortals' intervention. Record at least two details in each column with page numbers, paraphrasing or quoting exact words. Below the chart, write one sentence about what the details show about Percy and the risks he takes."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which details from pp. 327–333 show how much damage Percy takes, and what does that tell you about the risk he chooses?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"On p. 327 Ares's attacks throw Percy back and he has to keep getting up. The text shows he is hurt but keeps fighting, so he is risking serious injury to protect what matters to him."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How do Ares's attacks show the difference between a god and a demigod?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Ares can keep attacking with huge strength, like the moment Percy is catapulted on p. 327. Percy has to dodge and deflect, so he is outmatched in power and has to rely on skill and courage."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does the intervention of mortals change the fight, and why does the modern setting matter?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Ordinary people showing up changes how Ares acts, and he can't act freely in front of them. The modern setting means a god's battle has witnesses, which affects the outcome and shows that mortals matter in the story too."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does the fight show about how Percy has grown as a hero?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"At the start of the book he was unsure of himself, but here he takes a big risk and keeps going even when he is drained. That shows he is more confident and brave, and he fights for others, not just himself."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Check that students tie each claim to a page number and a specific detail. This misreads the fight; Ares is powerful and Percy is hurt and drained."},{"text":"He avoids the fight until the mortals arrive.","correct":false,"rationale":"Incorrect. This confuses the order of events; Percy faces Ares directly, and the mortals intervene during the fight."},{"type":"x","text":"He decides the fight is not worth the trouble.","correct":false,"rationale":"Incorrect. In Chapter 20 the buildup is the tension that leads into the fight, the confrontation is the battle itself, and the outcome is how the conflict with Ares ends. Looking at those parts shows how one scene fits into the whole plot."},{"type":"directions","text":"Create a three-box structure map labeled Buildup, Confrontation, and Outcome. In each box, write the key events from pp. 327–333 and one cited detail. Then write a 3–4 sentence paragraph explaining how this structure helps resolve the conflict with Ares. Use at least two vocabulary words from today."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Where does the buildup end and the confrontation begin on pp. 327–333?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The buildup is the tension before the first big hit. The confrontation starts when Ares attacks and Percy is catapulted on p. 327."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does the outcome resolve the conflict with Ares?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Ares is stopped and flees on p. 331, and Percy has reclaimed what was at stake on p. 332. That settles the problem that was building, though Percy is left drained."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Why is it important that this battle comes just before the end of the book?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It clears one big conflict before the final chapters, so the story can move toward the last challenge. It also shows Percy has grown enough to face what is coming."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Model paragraph (optional): The battle with Ares in Chapter 20 is built in three parts. At first the tension grows as Ares prepares to fight, and then in the confrontation Percy is catapulted back but keeps fighting. In the outcome, Ares fled and Percy reclaimed what was at stake, which resolves the conflict. This structure shows how Percy's growth leads to the resolution."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help students explain text structure and add details about time, manner, and cause with adverbials (ELD.PII.6.5) while evaluating the author's language choices (ELD.PI.6.7).","sayAsk":"Say: Tell your partner what happens first, next, and last. Ask: How did the author make the fight feel tense? Frames: At first ___. Then, suddenly ___. In the end ___ because ___. The word ___ makes the moment feel ___.","watchFor":"If students list events with no link to structure, then prompt: Which part of the scene is this? If students skip the outcome, then ask: How does the conflict end? Success: students name all three parts and explain how they connect."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.5"],"stem":"How does the outcome of the fight contribute to the plot of the novel?","choices":[{"text":"It resolves the conflict with Ares so the story can move toward its final challenges.","correct":true,"rationale":"Correct. The outcome settles this conflict and moves the plot forward."},{"text":"It introduces a brand-new conflict that has nothing to do with Ares.","correct":false,"rationale":"Incorrect. The outcome ends the conflict with Ares rather than starting an unrelated one."},{"text":"It shows that the battle did not matter to the plot.","correct":false,"rationale":"Incorrect. The battle resolves a major conflict, so it matters to the plot."},{"text":"It repeats the buildup without changing anything.","correct":false,"rationale":"Incorrect. The outcome changes the situation by ending the fight."}]},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: explaining how structure shapes the plot","tryThis":"Provide a completed buildup box and have students fill in the other two; use the frame The buildup creates ___, the confrontation shows ___, and the outcome ___."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to explain how the chapter would feel different if the mortals had not intervened, using evidence."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students answer the essential question and connect today's work to the Performance Task.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-reflection","title":"Modern Setting and the Battle","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.5"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Complete the sentences: The modern setting affects the battle between Percy and Ares by ___. One detail that shows this is the mortals' intervention on pp. 330–331.
